title: Telling stories & real conversation
goal: Tell a story, link events naturally, use relative clauses and reported speech, and sound natural with fillers and common expressions.
intro:
Sindhis are great storytellers — from grandmothers' tales to the epic love stories that Shah Abdul Latif turned into poetry. In this final unit you'll learn the glue of real conversation: story connectors (**هڪ ڀيري** 'once', **اوچتو** 'suddenly', **آخرڪار** 'in the end'), Sindhi's paired **relative clauses** (**جيڪو … سو** 'the one who … he'), **reported speech** with **ته**, and the fillers and expressions that make speech sound alive.

You'll also hear the pronoun endings from Unit 16 everywhere in stories: **چيائين** 'he/she said', **ڏٺائين** 'he/she saw'.

vocab.note: m. ڇا قصو آهي؟ = what's the story / what's going on?
f · pl ڳالهيون ɠālhyūṃ. ڳالهه ٻولهه = conversation.
Paired with تڏهن or ته: جڏهن … تڏهن …
Agrees: جيڪا (f), جيڪي (pl). Paired with سو / اهو.
f سا sā, pl سي se. Also 'so, therefore' at the start of a sentence.
Paired with اتي: جتي … اتي … Same spelling as جتي jutī 'shoe' (Unit 12).
جيئن توهان چئو = as you say / as you wish.
Starts questions softly: ڀلا، ڇا ٿيو؟ 'So, what happened?'
m. منهنجو مطلب آهي ته … = what I mean is …
m. Shah Latif's poetry is made of بيت and وايون (vāyūṃ, sung refrains).

phrases.roman: asula meṃ ɠālhi hīa āhe ta…

phrases.native: هن چيو ته هو سڀاڻي ايندو.
phrases.roman: hun chayo ta hū subhāṇe endo.

phrases.native: جيڪو ماڻهو ڪالهه آيو هو، سو منهنجو چاچو آهي.
phrases.roman: jeko māṇhū kālha āyo ho, so munhinjo chācho āhe.
phrases.en: The man who came yesterday is my uncle.

phrases.native: ٻڌ نه، هڪ مزيدار ڳالهه ٻڌايان.
phrases.roman: ɓudhu na, hika mazedāra ɠālhi ɓudhāyāṃ.
phrases.en: Listen, let me tell you something funny.

phrases.native: سچ پچ، مون کي کل اچي وئي.
phrases.roman: sach pach, moṃ khe khila achī vaī.

grammar.title: Relative clauses: جيڪو … سو, جتي … اتي, جڏهن … تڏهن
grammar.body:
Sindhi builds 'who / where / when' sentences in **pairs**: a **j-word** in the first clause and a matching **s- or t-word** (or a demonstrative) in the second:

**جيڪو … سو / اهو** — the one who … he: جيڪو محنت ڪري ٿو، سو ڪامياب ٿئي ٿو 'whoever works hard succeeds'
**جيڪا … سا** (f), **جيڪي … سي** (pl)
**جتي … اتي** — where … there
**جڏهن … تڏهن / ته** — when … then
**جيئن … تيئن** — as … so
**جيترو … اوترو** — as much … so much

The j-word agrees with the noun it refers to and takes the oblique before a postposition (جنهن 'whom, which (obl.)', جن 'whom (pl. obl.)'): جنهن ڪتاب جي مون ڳالهه ڪئي هئي … 'the book I talked about …'.

Story **connectors**: هڪ ڀيري 'once', پهريان 'first', پوءِ 'then', اوچتو 'suddenly', انهيءَ ڪري 'because of that', آخرڪار 'finally'.

examples.native: جيڪو ماڻهو دروازي تي آهي، سو ڪير آهي؟
examples.roman: jeko māṇhū darvāze te āhe, so ker āhe?
examples.en: Who's the man at the door? (lit. the man who is at the door, who is he?)

examples.native: جيڪا ڇوڪري ڳائي پئي، سا منهنجي ڀيڻ آهي.
examples.roman: jekā chhokirī ɠāe paī, sā munhinjī bheṇa āhe.
examples.en: The girl who's singing is my sister.

examples.native: جتي سنڌو درياهه آهي، اتي زندگي آهي.
examples.roman: jite sindhu daryāhu āhe, ute zindagī āhe.
examples.en: Where the Indus is, there is life.

examples.native: جڏهن مان ننڍو هوس، تڏهن ڳوٺ ۾ رهندو هوس.
examples.roman: jaɗahiṃ māṃ nanḍho hos, taɗahiṃ ɠoṭha meṃ rahando hos.
examples.en: When I was little, I used to live in the village. (man)

examples.native: جنهن ڪتاب جي مون ڳالهه ڪئي، اهو هي آهي.
examples.roman: janhin kitāba jī moṃ ɠālhi kaī, uho hī āhe.
examples.en: This is the book I talked about.

grammar.title: Reported speech with ته, and conversation glue
grammar.body:
Sindhi reports speech by repeating the speaker's words **as they were said**, after **ته** (ta) 'that': **هن چيو ته مان ٿڪل آهيان** — literally 'he said that I am tired' = he said he was tired. Pronouns may shift to fit the new speaker (as in English), but tenses usually stay as originally spoken.

Questions are reported the same way: هن پڇيو ته توهان ڪڏهن ايندا؟ 'she asked when you would come'. In stories you'll constantly hear **چيائين ته …** 'he/she said …' and **پڇيائين ته …** 'he/she asked …'.

**Conversation glue** — fillers and reactions:
ڀلا bhalā — well…, so… · يعني yaʿnī — I mean · ها ته hā ta — so anyway · ٻڌ نه / ٻڌو نه — listen… · واقعي؟ — really? · سچ پچ — honestly · ڇا ڳالهه آهي! — what a thing! / wow · خير — anyway, never mind.

**Idioms**: اکين تي 'gladly (lit. on my eyes)' · دل ٽٽڻ 'to be heartbroken (lit. heart breaks)' · ڪن ڏيڻ 'to listen closely (lit. give ear)' · هٿ ونڊائڻ 'to lend a hand'.

examples.native: هن چيو ته مان ٿڪل آهيان.
examples.roman: hun chayo ta māṃ thakalu āhiyāṃ.
examples.en: He said he was tired. (lit. said: I am tired)

examples.native: امان پڇيو ته توهان ماني کاڌي؟
examples.roman: amāṃ puchhyo ta tavhāṃ mānī khādhī?
examples.en: Mum asked whether you'd eaten. (lit. asked: did you eat?)
He said he'd definitely come tomorrow.

examples.native: ٻڌو نه، مون کي هڪ ڳالهه ياد آئي.
examples.roman: ɓudho na, moṃ khe hika ɠālhi yāda āī.

dialogue.title: The story of Sassui and Punhun
dialogue.setting: On a winter night in the courtyard, Grandmother (Nani) tells young Zubair a famous Sindhi love story.

lines.speaker: Zubair
lines.en: Nani, tell me a story, please!

lines.speaker: Nani
lines.native: ٻڌ. هڪ ڀيري ڀنڀور شهر ۾ سسئي نالي هڪ سهڻي ڇوڪري رهندي هئي.
lines.roman: ɓudhu. hika bhere bhanbhora shahara meṃ sasuī nāle hika sohaṇī chhokirī rahandī huī.
lines.en: Listen. Once, in the city of Bhambhore, there lived a beautiful girl named Sassui.

lines.speaker: Nani
lines.native: ڪيچ مڪران کان پنهون نالي هڪ شهزادو آيو. جڏهن سسئي کيس ڏٺو، تڏهن ٻنهي کي پيار ٿي ويو.
lines.roman: kecha makrāna khāṃ panhūṃ nāle hiku shahzādo āyo. jaɗahiṃ sasuī khesi ɗiṭho, taɗahiṃ ɓinhī khe pyāru thī vayo.
lines.en: From Kech Makran came a prince named Punhun. When Sassui saw him, the two fell in love.

lines.speaker: Nani
lines.native: پنهون جا ڀائر ناراض هئا. هڪ رات هنن پنهون کي بيهوش ڪيو ۽ اٺن تي کڻي ويا.
lines.roman: panhūṃ jā bhāura nārāzu huā. hika rāti hunan panhūṃ khe behoshu kayo ai uṭhan te khaṇī vayā.
lines.en: Punhun's brothers were angry. One night they drugged Punhun and carried him off on camels.

lines.speaker: Nani
lines.native: صبح جو سسئي اٿي ته پنهون ڪونه هو. هن جي دل ٽٽي پئي.
lines.roman: subuh jo sasuī uthī ta panhūṃ kona ho. hun jī dila ṭuṭī paī.
lines.en: In the morning Sassui woke up and Punhun was gone. Her heart broke.

lines.speaker: Nani
lines.native: هوءَ اڪيلي رڻ ۽ جبلن ۾ پنهون کي ڳولڻ نڪتي. چيائين ته پنهون کان سواءِ نه موٽنديس.
lines.roman: hūa akelī raṇa ai jabalan meṃ panhūṃ khe ɠolaṇa niktī. chayāīṃ ta panhūṃ khāṃ savāi na moṭandīs.
lines.en: She set out alone across the desert and mountains to find Punhun. She said she would not return without him.

lines.speaker: Zubair
lines.roman: ai āxirkāra hun khe panhūṃ milyo?
lines.en: And in the end, did she find Punhun?

lines.speaker: Nani
lines.native: چون ٿا ته جتي سسئي ڪري پئي، اتي ئي ٻنهي جو ميلاپ ٿيو — دنيا ۾ نه، پر روح ۾.
lines.roman: chavan thā ta jite sasuī kirī paī, ute ī ɓinhī jo melāpu thiyo — dunyā meṃ na, para rūha meṃ.
lines.en: They say that where Sassui fell, there the two were united — not in this world, but in spirit.

lines.speaker: Nani
lines.native: شاهه لطيف جو پيغام آهي ته سچو عاشق ڪڏهن به نٿو ٿڪجي.
lines.roman: shāh latīf jo paiġāmu āhe ta sacho ʿāshiqu kaɗahiṃ bi natho thakije.
lines.en: Shah Latif's message is that a true lover never tires.

lines.speaker: Zubair
lines.native: ڏاڍي اداس ڪهاڻي آهي، پر سهڻي آهي. مهرباني، ناني!
lines.roman: ɗāḍhī udāsu kahāṇī āhe, para sohaṇī āhe. meharbānī, nānī!
lines.en: It's a very sad story, but beautiful. Thank you, Nani!

culture: **Sassui and Punhun** is one of the great romances that Shah Abdul Latif wove into his *Risalo* as images of the soul's search for God; Sassui's lonely journey through the mountains is sung in the chapters 'Sur Sassui Abri', 'Sur Maazuri', 'Sur Desi', 'Sur Kohiyari' and 'Sur Husaini'. The ruins of **Bhambhore**, near Karachi, are linked to the legend. Other tales you'll hear in Sindh: **Umar–Marvi** (the village girl who refused a king's palace out of loyalty to her people in Thar), **Sohni–Mahiwal** (who swam the river on a clay pot), and **Moomal–Rano**. Knowing these stories — and a line or two of Latif — opens hearts everywhere in Sindh. *Mubārak!* You've finished the course.
